item.title: Law enforcement agencies tracking exam cheats, Omolo warns
item.dc:creator: CORRESPONDENT
item.description: "I want to appeal to our teachers. Please don't fall into the trap of those who want to make quick money by lying to you that they will steal for you examinations. Because when you do that, you're not just is ruining the lives of our children. You are ruining your life as a parent and also as a professional teacher and anyone who is deluded that they would want to take advantage," he stated.
item.content:encoded:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 11 – Interior Principal Secretary Raymond Omolo has warned individuals seeking to compromise national examinations that law enforcement agencies are tracking their activities.

Omolo has cautioned parents and teachers against paying individuals claiming they can obtain or leak examination papers, warning that such dealings could expose them to prosecution.

“I want to appeal to our teachers. Please don’t fall into the trap of those who want to make quick money by lying to you that they will steal for you examinations. Because when you do that, you’re not just is ruining the lives of our children. You are ruining your life as a parent and also as a professional teacher and anyone who is deluded that they would want to take advantage,” he stated.

He said those seeking to make quick money by exploiting anxious parents and learners were putting the future of children at risk.

The PS further warned teachers against participating in examination malpractice, saying they risk jeopardising their professional careers.

Omolo said the government had invested heavily in the education sector, including recruiting additional teachers, and would not allow examination fraud to undermine those efforts.

He urged parents and education stakeholders to support the integrity of the national examinations and avoid any attempts to secure unfair advantages for candidates.

item.title: Over 2.5mn learners take national assessments as KJSEA concludes
item.dc:creator: JEREMIAH WAKAYA
item.description: Attention now shifts to the main written Kenya Certificate of Secondary Education (KCSE) examinations, which begin on Monday, November 2.
item.content:encoded:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Oct 30 — More than 2.5 million learners participated in this week’s national assessments administered by the Kenya National Examinations Council (KNEC), Education Cabinet Secretary Julius Ogamba has said, as the Kenya Junior School Education Assessment (KJSEA) concludes Friday.

Ogamba said the assessments had generally progressed successfully across the country, despite isolated operational challenges involving adverse weather, administrative discrepancies and learners requiring special arrangements, including medical attention.

He said KNEC accorded all learners who presented themselves at their designated assessment centres the opportunity to sit their scheduled papers.

The CS commended education officials, security agencies and other stakeholders for their coordination in addressing the challenges, saying their efforts helped ensure that no learner was unnecessarily disadvantaged.

The conclusion of KJSEA marks a significant milestone for Grade 9 learners preparing to transition to Senior School in January 2027.

Ogamba said the assessment, alongside school-based assessments, would help determine learners’ next educational steps.

He assured parents and learners that the placement process would be orderly, transparent and equitable, taking into account performance, interests, pathway choices and other applicable considerations.

The Ministry of Education will communicate the relevant timelines and procedures through official channels, he said.

Attention now shifts to the main written Kenya Certificate of Secondary Education (KCSE) examinations, which begin on Monday, November 2, and run until November 20.

A total of 1,048,355 candidates have registered for the KCSE examinations, according to Ogamba, who urged education officials and security agencies to ensure examination centres are ready, personnel deployed and examination materials transported securely.

He also called for special attention to candidates with disabilities, those requiring medical attention and learners in areas affected by adverse weather or other challenging circumstances.

The CS said the government remained committed to ensuring that national assessments and examinations are conducted fairly, securely and with integrity while safeguarding the welfare of all learners.

item.title: KCA University opens 5th innovation week and Industry Summit
item.dc:creator: CORRESPONDENT
item.description: NAIROBI, Kenya, Oct 27 – Industry Principal Secretary Dr Juma Mukhwana and Bidco Africa Chairman Vimal Shah have urged Africa to stop exporting raw materials and start making its own…
item.content:encoded:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Oct 27 – Industry Principal Secretary Dr Juma Mukhwana and Bidco Africa Chairman Vimal Shah have urged Africa to stop exporting raw materials and start making its own products, as EU Ambassador to Kenya Andreas Peschke and KCA University Vice Chancellor Prof Isaiah Wakindiki pledged stronger support for young innovators.

The four spoke at the opening of the 5th KCA University Innovation Week and Industry Summit, held at the university’s Ruaraka campus under the theme Learn! Lead! Transform!

“No nation has become prosperous by consuming what other nations produce,” said Dr Mukhwana, who was the chief guest. “When we export raw materials, we import jobs.”

He noted that Africa has 1.4 billion people, about 18 percent of the world’s population, yet accounts for only around 3 percent of global manufacturing. “We export cotton and import clothes,” he said.
“Who will industrialise Africa? Africans must industrialise Africa. The solutions must come from you,” he told the students, challenging universities to turn research into commercial products, partner more closely with industry and produce entrepreneurs rather than job seekers.

Shah, who gave the keynote, said Kenya had no shortage of ideas. “The ideas are there. What we need is to become better at turning ideas into products, products into enterprises and enterprises into industries,” he said.

“A business begins with the real customer. Are they willing to pay for the value?” he posed, adding that innovation, not consumption, drives prosperity. “No country becomes prosperous by consuming. We need to innovate.”

With Africa’s population expected to reach 2.5 billion by 2050, he said the market was already waiting. “The demand is there. Consumption will keep happening. The question is, who is servicing the consumption?”

Prof Wakindiki said the university had secured more than Sh40 million in research grants, filed over 25 patent applications and supported eight startups in recent years.

“These are encouraging signs, but they also place a responsibility on us,” he said. “The quality of our journey will be judged by how well we connect research to users, and how consistently we stand with our innovators after the exhibition tents come down.”

He also cited EU-funded partnerships, including the Elevate AI project, which aims to equip more than 1,000 faculty and students in Kenya and Rwanda with artificial intelligence skills. “These partnerships are more than grants. They are bridges for knowledge,” he said.

Peschke said the summit came as the EU and Kenya celebrate 50 years of relations. “We have a strong partnership between the European Union and Kenya. EU support to entrepreneurship and to academic and scientific cooperation is important,” he said.

He pointed to programmes such as the Africa Mobility Scheme, which he said were designed to remove barriers facing Kenyan youth and help them support themselves.

“We are impressed by the spirit of entrepreneurship. This innovation week is very important, and whatever we can do as the European Union, we are going to do,” he said.

Student innovations on show include OmniSense, a remote equipment monitoring system; biodegradable diapers; a space tracking platform called Kessler Aegis; and Fortify AI, a business risk tool.

“The person who will build Kenya’s next great solution may be sitting next to you. It may be you,” Prof. Wakindiki told students.

The summit ends on Thursday.

item.title: Lecturers’ strike escalates as talks with govt collapse
item.dc:creator: DAVIS AYEGA
item.description: NAIROBI, Kenya Oct 12 – The ongoing lecturers’ strike in public universities is set to intensify after negotiations between university workers and the government collapsed on Monday raising the prospect…
item.content:encoded:
NAIROBI, Kenya Oct 12 – The ongoing lecturers’ strike in public universities is set to intensify after negotiations between university workers and the government collapsed on Monday raising the prospect of further disruption to learning.

The Universities Academic Staff Union (UASU) said the government presented an offer that was largely similar to the one tabled on October 1, which the union rejected as inadequate.

In a statement, UASU Secretary-General Constantine Wasonga said the meeting involving UASU, the Kenya Universities Staff Union (KUSU), KUDHEIHA and the government’s Inter-Ministerial Committee ended without an agreement.

“The talks have collapsed. The strike therefore continues,” Wasonga said, adding that the union would escalate its industrial action until its demands were addressed.

The union also faulted the National Treasury for failing to attend the meeting, saying its involvement was essential to resolving questions surrounding funding for staff salaries in public universities.

UASU is demanding a credible government offer and the conclusion of the 2025–2029 Collective Bargaining Agreement (CBA).

It also wants a firm commitment that the Exchequer will fund salaries for staff in public universities.

“Bringing back substantially the same offer is not meaningful engagement, and it does not demonstrate a commitment to resolve the dispute,” the union said.

The strike centres on the dispute over the 2025–2029 CBA, with university workers seeking an agreement on their employment terms and a clear government commitment to funding staff salaries.

The latest breakdown follows earlier negotiations, including a government proposal presented on October 1, which UASU says failed to meet its demands.

The union maintains that meaningful progress will require a revised offer and a clear plan for financing public university salaries.

UASU has urged staff in public universities to remain united as it presses the government to reach an agreement.

item.title: Cost, skills gaps hold back assistive technology access in Africa
item.dc:creator: PHIDEL KIZITO
item.category: WHO-UNICEF Global Report on Assistive Technology
item.description: NAIROBI, Kenya, Oct 8 – High costs and shortages of skilled personnel are limiting access to assistive technology across Africa, leaving millions of people without products that could improve their…
item.content:encoded:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Oct 8 – High costs and shortages of skilled personnel are limiting access to assistive technology across Africa, leaving millions of people without products that could improve their ability to work, learn and live independently.

The challenge is becoming an increasingly important economic issue as governments seek to expand access to spectacles, hearing aids, wheelchairs and other devices that support participation in education and employment.

The WHO-UNICEF Global Report on Assistive Technology estimates that more than 2.5 billion people globally need at least one assistive product, while nearly one billion are unable to access them. In some low-income settings, services meet as little as three percent of demand.

The World Health Organization identifies high prices, weak financing, limited product availability, fragmented services and shortages of trained personnel among the main barriers to access.

The skills shortage is particularly pronounced in eye care, where basic vision correction is among the largest areas of assistive technology need.

Data from the International Agency for the Prevention of Blindness shows that Sub-Saharan Africa has a median of only two optometrists per million people, compared with 156 per million in high-income regions.

In a 21-country regional study, the availability of optometrists outside capital cities fell to 0.9 per million people, highlighting the difficulty of delivering basic refractive services to rural and underserved communities.

The shortage means patients with straightforward vision needs can face long distances and additional costs to access services, while limited specialist capacity can make it harder for health systems to address demand at scale.

“Global commitments matter, but access becomes real only when a person can get the right product, at a price they can afford, close to where they live. That last mile is where policy becomes participation,” said Bradley Heslop and Adam Boxer, Co-CEOs of Dot Glasses.

“This World Sight Day, we are calling on governments, health systems, funders, employers and communities to each play their part in removing the barriers that still keep people from basic eye care,” they added.

The issue has gained renewed global attention following the adoption of United Nations General Assembly Resolution 80/305 in September, the first UNGA resolution specifically dedicated to access to assistive technology.

Sponsored by 41 member states and adopted without a vote, the resolution seeks to place affordable and quality assistive technology more firmly within universal health coverage and sustainable development.

For Africa, implementation will require more than policy commitments, with governments needing to address financing, procurement, workforce training, distribution and maintenance of assistive products.

The economic stakes extend beyond healthcare. Poor access to vision correction, mobility devices and hearing technology can affect school attendance, workplace participation and productivity, increasing the wider cost of exclusion.

item.title: Crawford links Kenyan students to 104 global universities
item.dc:creator: CORRESPONDENT
item.description: NAIROBI, Kenya, Oct 2 – More than 700 students and parents from 13 schools attended a university fair in Nairobi that brought together representatives from over 104 universities from Europe,…
item.content:encoded:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Oct 2 – More than 700 students and parents from 13 schools attended a university fair in Nairobi that brought together representatives from over 104 universities from Europe, the United States, Asia and Australia.

The fair, hosted by Crawford International School at its Tatu City campus on September 25 in partnership with Uniserv Education, provided students with information on university admissions, scholarships, visas and accommodation for those seeking to study abroad.

Students engaged directly with university representatives on entry requirements, available courses and alternative degree programmes, including combined courses in areas such as law and international relations.

The event also provided information on financial aid, merit-based grants and partial and full scholarships, as students and parents weighed the cost of pursuing higher education outside Kenya.

“The world does not reward knowledge alone; it rewards what young people can do with that knowledge”.

The fair also covered visa application requirements, accommodation and opportunities for internships, student exchanges and cultural immersion programmes.

Crawford said its graduates have secured placements at more than 120 international universities, highlighting the growing role of schools in helping students navigate overseas higher education options.

The event comes as Kenyan students increasingly consider international universities as part of their higher education plans, with access to information on admissions, financing and immigration requirements becoming an important part of the decision-making process.

The participation of parents also brought discussions around tuition costs, relocation and longer-term career planning into the university selection process.

The fair was open beyond Crawford students, with learners from other international and national schools attending the event.

item.title: UASU issues seven-day strike notice over stalled lecturers’ CBA
item.dc:creator: JEREMIAH WAKAYA
item.description: UASU has issued a seven-day notice for a nationwide lecturers’ strike starting October 2 over the stalled 2025–2029 CBA
item.content:encoded:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Sep 24 — The Universities Academic Staff Union (UASU) has issued a seven-day notice for a nationwide strike by lecturers, with the industrial action set to begin at midnight on October 2.

The union said the decision follows what it described as the persistent failure by university councils, the Ministry of Education and the National Treasury to honour the Return-to-Work Formula signed on November 5, 2025.

UASU also said the government has failed to provide a financial counter-proposal for the 2025–2029 Collective Bargaining Agreement (CBA).

“While other employees in the public education sector concluded their 2025–2029 CBAs last year, lecturers in public universities have been abandoned,” the union said on Thursday.

The notice follows a disclosure by the Salaries and Remuneration Commission (SRC) on September 21 that neither the Ministry of Education nor the National Treasury had provided a written commitment that funding for public universities’ CBAs would be provided through the National Exchequer.

UASU said the SRC consequently could not issue the constitutional advice required to facilitate financial counter-proposals to the unions.

“This disclosure by SRC confirms that the negotiations held at Machakos University since last year have been an exercise in futility,” UASU said.

The union also objected to what it said was a government position that funding for public university lecturers could be drawn from student fees and market-based funding.

“UASU rejects this position firmly. Academic staff in public universities are public officers.”

The union argued that lecturers’ remuneration should be secured from the National Exchequer, citing the constitutional definition of public office and the requirement that remuneration and benefits be payable from the Consolidated Fund or money provided by Parliament.

UASU also criticised reliance on social media statements regarding the proposed new university funding model.

“Unions cannot be directed to rely on social media declarations or to interpret the implied meanings in the proposed Tertiary Education Placement and Funding Bill, 2026, which Parliament has not enacted,” the union said.

It questioned whether public universities were being shifted towards a market-based funding model, asking: “Do we still have public universities or have they changed to market based universities?”

UASU’s demands

The union wants the 2025–2029 CBA negotiated, signed, registered and implemented, with the Ministry of Education and National Treasury providing a commitment that it will be funded through the National Exchequer.

It is also demanding that the Government cease attempts to remove the public officer status of public university lecturers and that the proposed tertiary education funding legislation explicitly safeguard their remuneration from the Exchequer.

UASU further wants to participate in the development of human-resource instruments for public universities currently being developed by the Public Service Commission.

The union said fair remuneration of academic staff is critical to public university education and the future of students.

“A dignified, fairly remunerated academic staff is critical for the quality of public university education, the safe guarding the future of students, and the socioeconomic development of Kenya,” UASU said.

item.title: Prof Wakindiki: Kenya’s Universities have three years to rethink how they teach
item.dc:creator: CONTRIBUTOR
item.description: NAIROBI, Kenya, Sept 24 – The students who will arrive at Kenyan universities in 2029 will have spent their entire schooling being asked not what they know, but what they can…
item.content:encoded:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Sept 24 – The students who will arrive at Kenyan universities in 2029 will have spent their entire schooling being asked not what they know, but what they can do. The institutions waiting for them have three years to learn to ask the same thing.

That was the warning from Prof Isaiah I.C Wakindiki, the vice chancellor of KCA University, at an inaugural lecture in Nairobi on Wednesday.

More than 1.13 million learners in the pioneer cohort of Kenya’s Competency-Based Education system are expected at university that year, he said.

“If competency is to become the organising principle of Kenyan higher education, someone must do the hard intellectual work of showing how,” Prof Wakindiki said.

Prof Anne Syomwene Kisilu, the dean of the School of Education, Arts and Social Sciences, offered a framework she calls the Competency Transformation Model.

Universities cannot succeed by adjusting isolated parts of the system, she argued. What is taught, how it is taught, how learning is assessed, who teaches and how institutions work with industry must all change at once.

The model lists ten dimensions, from an evidence-based needs assessment to the retraining of faculty, and its slides insist they are not sequential steps. Change in one, the presentation said, requires change in the others. The intended result is a graduate with fourteen named attributes, including critical thinking, digital competence, ethical reasoning and entrepreneurship.

Its sharpest demand falls on examinations. “We must move from recall-based examinations to real-world, performance-based tasks that show learners can apply their competences in meaningful contexts,” Prof Kisilu said. Projects, portfolios, case analyses and simulations would replace tests of memory.

Lecturers would also change roles, from subject experts to facilitators, coaches, mentors and learning designers, which Prof Kisilu said makes continuous retraining of staff indispensable.

She urged universities to invest in laboratories, innovation hubs, simulation facilities and internships, to bring employers into curriculum design and assessment, and to replace periodic curriculum reviews with a continuous, evidence-based cycle.

The proposals raise questions of cost and pace that a lecture is not built to answer. Laboratories and retrained staff are expensive, Kenya’s universities differ widely in their means, and how many of the 1.13 million will choose universities over other routes remains a separate question.

Prof Wakindiki cautioned that a university is not measured by its assets. “Programmes, buildings and technology tell the world what a university has,” he said. “But scholarly excellence tells the world what a university is.

item.title: Universities urged to rebuild public trust through accountability and relevance
item.dc:creator: PHIDEL KIZITO
item.description: NAIROBI, Kenya,Sep 15 — Universities need to treat public trust as an institutional asset and demonstrate their value through accountability, research and responsiveness to economic needs, academics and government officials have…
item.content:encoded:
NAIROBI, Kenya,Sep 15 — Universities need to treat public trust as an institutional asset and demonstrate their value through accountability, research and responsiveness to economic needs, academics and government officials have said.

The call emerged from a roundtable on restoring trust in academia and the knowledge economy convened by Strathmore University and the State Department for Foreign Affairs on Tuesday ahead of the Trust Summit scheduled for October.

Speakers argued that declining confidence in universities should not be addressed solely through public relations, but through stronger systems, transparent decision-making and research that responds to challenges facing businesses, governments and communities.

Prof Gilbert Kokwaro, Director of the Institute of Healthcare Management at Strathmore University Business School, said universities should consider trust alongside financial, physical, intellectual and human capital.

“Trust is earned. It is not received. A university does not receive trust because it is prestigious. It earns trust through the integrity of its scholarship, the quality of its relationships, the fairness of its decisions, and the transparency with which it uses its authority and its resources.”

“Trust is ultimately earned through conduct. Institutions build it by producing reliable knowledge, maintaining high standards, responding to societal needs and being accountable for the quality and impact of their work,” said Dr Korir Sing’Oei, Principal Secretary, State Department for Foreign Affairs, in remarks delivered on his behalf.

The discussion also highlighted a mismatch between higher education output and labour-market demand.

Prof Sarah Ssali, First Deputy Vice Chancellor for Academic Affairs at Makerere University, said graduate employment figures should not be used alone to determine the value of university education, arguing that wider economic conditions influence employment outcomes.

“In Uganda, we graduate around 40,000 students per year across all universities, public and private, but only 700 jobs are being created per year,” she said, adding that the problem reflected a mismatch between demand and supply rather than necessarily the value of degrees.

Strathmore University Vice Chancellor Dr Vincent Ogutu challenged researchers to focus on unresolved problems in industry and communities and demonstrate measurable value.

The issue has wider implications for the knowledge economy as universities compete for students, research funding, industry partnerships and public confidence.

A 2025 study published in Nature Human Behaviour, involving nearly 72,000 respondents across 68 countries, found a gap between perceptions of scientists’ competence and their willingness to listen to wider public views.

The Nairobi discussions will feed into the Information Integrity and Trust in the Digital Age agenda of the Trust Summit, scheduled for October 21–23, 2026.

item.title: Epson targets Africa’s power-constrained SMEs with low-energy technology
item.dc:creator: PHIDEL KIZITO
item.description: NAIROBI, Kenya, Sept 1 – Epson is stepping up its push into Africa’s small business and emerging markets, targeting enterprises and consumers seeking to cut operating costs as unreliable electricity…
item.content:encoded:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Sept 1 – Epson is stepping up its push into Africa’s small business and emerging markets, targeting enterprises and consumers seeking to cut operating costs as unreliable electricity and high energy prices continue to shape technology choices.

The Japanese technology company says growing digitalization across Africa is creating demand for printing and projection equipment that can operate efficiently in markets where continuous power supply cannot always be guaranteed.

Epson President for Africa, Middle East and West and Central Asia Neil Colquhoun said the company sees an opportunity in Africa’s largely small and medium-sized business economy, where affordability, energy efficiency and ease of use can influence technology adoption.

“Our target market is very large because if we go into more rural locations in Africa, where sometimes you have to use an inverter or solar, you can still use Epson technology.”

The company is promoting its Heat-Free PrecisionCore printing technology, which it says can consume substantially less power than conventional laser systems, alongside ink-tank printers designed to reduce reliance on frequent cartridge purchases.

Colquhoun said the approach is particularly relevant for SMEs, schools and households operating in areas where electricity costs and reliability remain concerns.

“We want to have high-quality products, with low power consumption and low intervention, so customers can essentially forget about the product and get on with their business.”

Epson’s regional business has recorded about 20 percent year-on-year growth, according to the company, with demand spanning consumer and business printing, scanning, projection and professional printing.

The firm is also seeking to strengthen local partnerships and increase its brand presence as it expands in Africa, South America, Southeast Asia, the Middle East and Turkey.

As part of the expansion, Epson has opened a new 250-square-metre office in Nairobi that will serve as its East African base and include a demonstration facility where customers can test its technology.

Colquhoun said the Nairobi operation would allow Epson to better understand regional customer needs, with the company open to developing products specifically tailored to East and West African markets.

The strategy reflects a broader opportunity for technology manufacturers in emerging markets, where the ability to deliver lower-cost, energy-efficient equipment could prove as important as advanced features in winning customers.
